title: SMaCk: Efficient Instruction Cache Attacks via Self-Modifying Code Conflicts
problem: Self-modifying code (SMC) detection on x86 processors triggers pipeline flushes and machine clears that are shared between SMT sibling threads, creating measurable timing side channels on the L1 instruction cache that are significantly more distinguishable (150-350 cycle differences) than conventional L1i cache Prime+Probe attacks (1-2 cycle differences). These SMC-based timing channels have not been systematically exploited as a standalone attack primitive for information leakage.
motivation: Conventional L1i cache side-channel attacks suffer from low signal-to-noise ratios because cache hit/miss timing differences are only 1-2 cycles; SMC pipeline flushes amplify this signal 100-350x, enabling more reliable cryptographic key extraction and covert channels.
method: When code modifies instructions already in the L1 instruction cache, the x86 processor pauses and clears its pipeline—discarding all unfinished work to stay correct—adding 235–425 observable clock cycles. Researchers identified which instructions cause this pause (clflush, clflushopt, store, lock+inc, prefetch, clwb), then built attacks called Prime+iProbe and Flush+iReload that exploit the delay: they fill the cache with dummy instructions and measure the delay spike when victim code evicts them, leaking which instructions the victim ran. In practice, they recovered 70% of a 2048-bit RSA key from 10 measurements, extracted encryption keys from OpenSSL servers in a single measurement (65–90% recovery), and built a Spectre-v1 variant that achieves up to 4,105 bytes/second throughput.
key_novelty: This paper shows how to exploit the x86 processor's self-modifying code detection mechanism as a side channel on the L1 instruction cache, producing 100–350 times larger timing signals than previous attacks and enabling information theft between unprivileged sibling threads.
contributions: Systematic characterization of which x86 instructions trigger the SMC detection mechanism and their timing profiles across Intel and AMD microarchitectures
Prime+iProbe and Flush+iReload L1i cache attack variants leveraging SMC timing, achieving up to 670 Kbit/s covert channel bandwidth with <1% error rate
End-to-end cryptographic attacks: 2048-bit RSA key recovery in 10 traces and single-trace OpenSSL SRP server key extraction with up to 90% bit leakage
ISpectre: a Spectre-v1 variant using L1i cache encoding that bypasses data-cache-focused Spectre defenses
Performance counter-based dynamic detection with 99.36% F-score using machine_clears.smc counter

metrics.other: Covert channel: up to 670 Kbit/s, <1% error rate (Flush+iFlush/Flushopt); RSA key recovery: 70% bits in 10 traces (Prime+iFlush) vs. state-of-the-art Mastik; SRP leakage: 65-90% bits in single trace vs. 22-48% for Mastik; ISpectre throughput: up to 4105 B/s on AMD Ryzen 5; detection F-score: 0.987

baselines: Lipp et al. AMD cache attack (0.66 B/s)
limitations: Attack requires SMT (hyper-threading) to be enabled; effectiveness varies across microarchitectures (e.g., AMD EPYC 7232P resists flush-based SMC conflicts); ~45% of SRP key bits remain unrecoverable per single trace due to sliding window ambiguity.
primary_theme: L1 instruction cache side-channel attacks via self-modifying code pipeline flushes
